## Introduction

Cutaneous beta- and gamma-HPVs act more like normal skin flora than disease-causing pathogens. They are acquired early in life, are ubiquitous in healthy adults, and persist as asymptomatic, low-level infections [@antonsson2000; @doorbar2023] that expand when host immunity fails [@hou2026]. At the DNA level, this viral reservoir is large and well mapped. Shotgun metagenomics detected HPV in 61.3% of healthy skin samples [@ma2014], and skin swabs found beta-HPV in 92% of adults [@rollison2019sites]. The community is highly diverse, spanning 396 distinct types, 229 of which were previously unknown [@bzhalava2014]. However, DNA detection alone cannot show whether any of these viral genomes are transcribed.

This question matters because beta-HPV is a suspected cofactor in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), particularly in organ transplant recipients [@howley2015; @rollison2019]. Three distinct, mutually compatible theories explain this role using the same data. Under the "hit-and-run" model, beta-HPV works with ultraviolet radiation, immunosuppression, or chronic inflammation during early cancer development but becomes dispensable once the tumor forms [@viarisio2018; @dorfer2021]. This model claims only that the virus is no longer required, not that it is lost, so it predicts a decline in viral activity only if there is a route to loss. For example, ultraviolet-induced mutations in host genes such as *TP53* or *NOTCH* may make the viral oncogenes redundant, so that the viral genome is no longer selected for [@viarisio2018]. Alternatively, the protective-immunity theory suggests that T-cell immunity to commensal papillomaviruses actively suppresses skin cancer, meaning that viral loss reflects immune selection [@strickley2019; @lambert2021; @strickley2021]. This idea now includes evidence that viral colonization blocks the expansion of mutant p53 clones, with beta-HPV disappearing as those clones grow [@son2025]. A third theory requires neither premise. It proposes that silence is simply the viral default, because the beta-HPV genome uses E8\^E2 to repress its own expression and cell transformation requires inactivating this repressor [@rehm2022]. All three models therefore predict declining viral activity from healthy skin to carcinoma, so measuring that decline more precisely cannot distinguish between them.

Studies that tested directly whether HPV is transcribed in cutaneous carcinoma have mostly found little or no viral transcription. The original cSCC transcriptome study found none [@arron2011], and neither did a study of 12 skin lesions sequenced to a median of 66 million reads [@hultin2019]. A study of 345 posttransplant tumors at 35 million reads found transcription in only 15 cases [@arroyomuhr2021], and a study of 23 risk-stratified biopsies detected no viral transcripts despite a 64% DNA positivity rate [@vandiver2021]. E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization supports these findings, showing expression in 0.9% of 225 nonanogenital cSCCs [@fujimoto2019]. The literature is not unanimous, however: in situ hybridization detected transcripts of HPV types associated with epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) in 4 of 11 PCR-positive transplant cSCCs [@purdie2005]. These studies share a limitation. Most examined lesions alone, so they cannot say how often HPV is transcribed in carcinoma relative to skin without disease. Sample sizes were small, from 11 to 345 specimens, and four of the five studies had no comparison group of unselected skin. The largest study was limited to formalin-fixed transplant material, and none scored productive replication.

Public sequencing archives make such a comparison possible. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) studies of human tissue usually align reads to the human genome and discard the reads that do not match it. Viral reads are among those discarded, but they remain in the raw data deposited in public archives and can be recovered by reanalysis [@edgar2022]. This approach has already been applied to skin [@leiendecker2023; @bhargava2025]. It has pitfalls, however. HeLa-derived HPV18 contaminates archived data extensively [@cantalupo2015; @kazemian2015; @adey2013], and sequencing depth and library chemistry both limit what any survey can reliably detect. Here, we reanalyzed public human RNA-seq data spanning healthy skin, warts, and skin cancer to ask how often cutaneous HPV is transcribed, which types are present, and whether the infection is productive.
